title: Butchering a rabbit for the freezer
subtitle: Skinning, gutting, and jointing a home-reared rabbit.
excerpt: A home-reared rabbit processed humanely at the right weight gives some of the best-value lean meat from a smallholding. Processing takes around 20 minutes once you know the steps. The key skills are a clean kill, a neat pelt removal, and a careful gut-out that avoids contaminating the carcass.
sourceNotes: Bob Bennett, Storey's Guide to Raising Rabbits (5th edn., 2009), processing chapter. Carla Emery, Encyclopedia of Country Living (9th edn., 1994), rabbits section. Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall, River Cottage Meat Book (2004), rabbit chapter.

glossaryTerms.definition: The humane method of killing a rabbit by sharply separating the first cervical vertebra from the skull. Instant loss of consciousness when performed correctly.
Removing the stomach and intestines from a rabbit carcass. The step that requires the most care to avoid gut puncture.

content.text: Butchering a rabbit for home consumption is legal in the UK without any licence. The rabbit should be processed at 8 to 12 weeks of age (fryer weight) or up to 5 to 6 months (roaster weight). A fryer weighs 1.8 to 2.3 kg live; a roaster 2.7 to 3.6 kg. Older rabbits still eat well but need longer, slower cooking.

is the standard method for a competent operator. Hold the rabbit firmly by the hind legs with one hand, place the other hand over the top of the head with the thumb behind the skull. Push the head sharply downward and backward in a single decisive movement. The vertebra dislocates and the rabbit loses consciousness instantly. If you are not confident performing this, ask an experienced stockkeeper to demonstrate before you try alone.
Hang the carcass by the hind legs from a hook or beam. Work immediately while the carcass is still warm, as the pelt removes more cleanly.
Cut through the hock joints on the hind legs with kitchen scissors. Cut the tail and the front feet at the knee.

Make a cut through the fur and skin only (do not cut into the muscle) around the hind legs, then grip the pelt firmly and pull downward toward the head. It should come away in one piece. If it resists, use the knife tip to free it from the carcass before pulling again.
Pull the pelt completely off over the head and discard or set aside for tanning.
is the step that requires the most care. A punctured gut contaminates the meat and produces a strong smell.
Pinch the belly skin and make a small cut with the knife tip just below the sternum. Work the knife blade upward, cutting away from the gut, to open the belly cavity from sternum to pelvis.
Reach in and pull the stomach, intestines, bladder, and reproductive organs out in one connected mass. Cut the rectum free at the pelvis to release everything.

The liver, kidneys, and heart are excellent to eat. The liver should be smooth and evenly coloured. Dark spots or a mottled appearance indicates liver fluke or other infection; discard the whole carcass if in doubt.

Rinse the body cavity with cold water and pat dry. Refrigerate for 1 to 2 days before freezing or cooking; a brief rest improves texture. Freeze in whole, half, or jointed portions. A jointed rabbit (hind legs, saddle, front legs) is the most practical form for home cooking.

attrs.cue: Gut was nicked during paunching and the contents spilled
attrs.cause: Knife tip cut too deep or worked too fast
attrs.fix: Rinse the cavity thoroughly with cold water. If only a small spill, the meat is still usable. A large rupture of the caecum (the large fermentation chamber) is harder to clean; rinse repeatedly and cook soon rather than freezing.

attrs.cue: Pelt tears during removal and hair gets on the meat
attrs.cause: Skin not cut cleanly or pulled at too sharp an angle
attrs.fix: Remove visible hair with a wet cloth. Shave the contaminated area with the knife. Hair does not affect safety but is unpleasant to eat.
